input: Test the thesis: data-center power demand supports Vistra's growth over the next 3 years

output.thesis: Data-center power demand supports Vistra's growth over the next 3 years (2027-2029): surging load in ERCOT and PJM — Vistra's two core markets — plus long-term data-center-linked contracts (Meta, Comanche Peak PPA, Helix/New Era) and tight capacity markets drive rising realized energy and capacity prices and multi-year EBITDA growth.
output.verdict: Partly supported, leaning supported. The evidence strongly shows data-center-driven demand growth in Vistra's core ERCOT and PJM markets is already converting into contracted growth — 2,609 MW of 20-year Meta nuclear PPAs, a 1,200 MW Comanche Peak PPA, the Helix/NVIDIA preferred-power role, ~10.6 GW cleared in PJM at $333.44/MW-day, and initiated 2027 EBITDA guidance of $7.7-$8.5 billion (up from $5.7-$5.9 billion guided for 2025). But the 3-year earnings path is substantially hedged and contract-locked rather than data-center-price-sensitive, regulatory price caps and political risk limit upside in PJM, demand forecasts carry 5x error bars, and part of the recent EBITDA surge reflects weather and acquisitions rather than data-center demand — so the thesis supports growth, while the magnitude attributable specifically to data-center demand over exactly 3 years is uncertain.

evidence_for.claim: Vistra signed 20-year PPAs with Meta for a total of 2,609 MW of carbon-free nuclear energy and capacity from three PJM plants (2,176 MW from operating Perry and Davis-Besse plants plus 433 MW of incremental uprate capacity at Perry, Davis-Besse and Beaver Valley), with purchases beginning late 2026 — the largest nuclear uprates supported by a corporate customer in the U.S.

Vistra projects the Meta agreements to add approximately 8%-10% incremental adjusted free cash flow accretion from operating energy and capacity plus an additional 5%-7% from uprate capacity (assuming full delivery and 2026 adjusted FCFbG guidance), with ~80% EBITDA-to-FCF conversion on incremental EBITDA.

Vistra signed a 20-year PPA (options to extend up to 20 more years) with a large, investment-grade customer to supply 1,200 MW of carbon-free power from Comanche Peak Nuclear Power Plant, with delivery anticipated to begin Q4 2027 and ramp to full capacity by 2032; NRC has extended Comanche Peak's operation through 2053.

Q3 2026 Ongoing Operations Adjusted EBITDA of $2,378 million, up more than 50% ($797 million) vs Q3 2025, driven primarily by higher realized energy and capacity prices, Lotus plants contribution and Martin Lake Unit 1's return; Vistra raised 2026 Ongoing Operations Adjusted EBITDA guidance to $7.1-$7.5 billion and initiated 2027 guidance of $7.7-$8.5 billion (Adjusted FCFbG $4.3-$5.1 billion).

Vistra cleared ~10,566 MW in the PJM capacity auction for the 2027/2028 planning year at a weighted average clearing price of $333.44/MW-day, locking in capacity revenue into 2028; it had cleared ~10,314 MW at $329.17/MW-day in the 2026/2027 auction (July 2025).

Vistra closed the Cogentrix Energy acquisition in October 2026, adding ~5,500 MW of natural gas-fueled generation (~$2.2 billion cash plus repayment of ~$1.7 billion assumed debt), expanding its dispatchable fleet for large-load/data-center demand.

EIA (Feb 2026 STEO) forecasts the fastest US load growth in ERCOT and PJM — Vistra's core markets — averaging 10% and 3% respectively between 2025 and 2027, driven by data centers; in a high-demand scenario the ERCOT 2027 wholesale price averages $37/MWh (79%) above baseline, while ERCOT gas generation rises ~105 BkWh.

Vistra announced Helix Digital Infrastructure alongside NVIDIA, KKR and Kuwait Investment Authority, with an initial Vistra commitment of up to $1.0 billion and Vistra as Helix's preferred power provider — a direct channel to AI data-center demand.

Vistra completed the acquisition of seven natural gas plants from Lotus Infrastructure Partners (~2,600 MW) and took final investment decision to build two new Permian Basin gas units totaling 860 MW (Sept 2025) 'to meet West Texas' growing power needs', citing data-center build-out among its demand drivers (CEO Jim Burke).

Vistra signed a 20-year 207 MW PPA with New Era Energy and Digital at its Odessa combined-cycle gas plant in Texas (data-center-adjacent large-load customer), and commenced operations of the 405 MW Pulaski Solar Facility under a PPA with Microsoft.
As of Oct 30, 2026, Vistra had hedged ~100% of expected generation volumes for 2026, ~98% for 2027 and ~78% for 2028, materially de-risking the 3-year earnings path.

Vistra's board authorized an additional $1.5 billion of share repurchases (~$2.5 billion total remaining through year-end 2028); ~$6.7 billion repurchased since Nov 2021 and shares outstanding down ~30%, amplifying per-share growth from the EBITDA ramp.

Texas data-center grid demand is expected to exceed 40 GW by 2028 (vs ~8 GW maximum demand in 2025), with Texas forecast to become the largest US data-center market within two years — a direct tailwind for Vistra's Texas (ERCOT) segment.

missing_fields: Exact contract pricing/revenue of the Meta 2,609 MW and Comanche Peak 1,200 MW PPAs (not disclosed in retrieved sources)
Vistra-specific data-center revenue or MW share quantified by the company (contracts are disclosed as MW and accretion %, not revenue)
2028 guidance (not yet initiated as of the Q3 2026 release, Nov 6, 2026)
counterarguments: The growth is already largely contracted and hedged, not incremental upside: with ~98% of 2027 generation hedged and capacity revenues locked at administratively capped prices ($329.17-$333.44/MW-day under PJM's FERC-approved cap-and-collar), further data-center demand may not lift earnings above the $7.7-$8.5 billion 2027 guidance unless new contracts (like Meta's) are signed.

Regulatory/political intervention cuts both ways: PJM's price cap and floor were imposed because of data-center-driven bill increases (1.5-5% retail bill impacts), and Jefferies flags growing political risk in Texas and PJM — the same demand that drives Vistra's pricing invites caps, market redesign or reliability-must-run interventions that compress the upside.

The data-center demand forecasts underpinning the thesis have huge error bars: Wood Mackenzie sees only ~23 GW of realistic AI buildout vs 90+ GW of requests, 2030 forecasts vary 5x, and about a third of data centers may self-supply power by 2030 — if load growth disappoints, ERCOT price upside (the single biggest swing factor in EIA's scenarios) disappears.

Valuation and balance sheet: InvestingPro fair-value estimates flag the stock as overvalued and Moody's moved its outlook back to stable on acquisition-driven leverage, so even if demand materializes, per-share upside may be limited and credit quality could constrain further growth capex.

Part of the reported growth is not data-center demand at all: Q3 2026's 50%+ EBITDA jump was driven by weather (one of the hottest Q3s on record, all-time ERCOT/PJM peak demand records), the Lotus/Cogentrix acquisitions and Martin Lake's return — sources that do not recur, and mild weather already cut retail EBITDA in Q1 2026.

evidence_against.claim: PJM's 2026/2027 capacity auction cleared at a federally approved price cap of $329.17/MW-day with a floor of $175/MW-day, agreed after Pennsylvania Governor Shapiro's December 2024 FERC complaint — regulatory intervention caps the upside Vistra can capture from PJM capacity scarcity.

EIA's high-demand scenario shows price upside is concentrated in ERCOT (+79% in 2027) while PJM prices rise only ~4% because interconnections with other regions mute the effect; higher gas demand also implies ~$0.50/MMBtu higher delivered gas costs, a margin headwind on Vistra's gas fleet.

Wood Mackenzie estimates a realistic AI data-center buildout of only ~23 GW nationally vs 90+ GW of utility interconnection requests, and 2030 data-center demand forecasts vary 5x (200-1,050 TWh/yr, WRI/BCG) — utility/queue-based load forecasts may be materially overstated.

About one-third of data centers are expected to have onsite power generation by 2030 (e.g., natural gas engines, fuel cells), bypassing the grid — a structural risk to merchant generators' ability to monetize data-center load.

Moody's revised Vistra's outlook from positive to stable, citing its acquisitive strategy and delayed deleveraging; the Meta nuclear uprate program's capex (<20% of total spend by end-2028, most falling 2028-2034) means much of the uprate benefit lands outside the 3-year window.

Jefferies downgraded Vistra to Hold (Sept 22, 2025), citing growing political risks in Texas and PJM and concerns about ERCOT system reliability delays — political/regulatory pushback on high power prices is a live risk in exactly the markets driving the thesis.

InvestingPro Fair Value estimates put Vistra (shares ~$169.35, market cap ~$57 billion at the time) as overvalued despite its strong financial profile — much of the data-center growth may already be priced in.

Q1 2026 Retail segment Adjusted EBITDA fell to $68 million from $184 million a year earlier on mild Texas weather, showing results remain weather-exposed quarter to quarter even as data-center-driven growth builds.
Vistra recorded a $269 million partial impairment of the Moss Landing 350 facility in Q3 2026 — execution/asset-risk in its West segment alongside the growth story.

key_uncertainties: Whether the ~90 GW of requested data-center load (vs Wood Mackenzie's ~23 GW realistic estimate) actually materializes; granular ERCOT/PJM interconnection-queue attrition data and utility large-load tariff filings would resolve it.

PJM capacity-market design after the 2027/2028 auction — whether the FERC-approved cap ($329.17) and floor ($175) regime is extended or replaced, which directly sets Vistra's ~10.5 GW of PJM capacity revenue.
Pricing of the Meta (2,609 MW) and Comanche Peak (1,200 MW) 20-year PPAs is not disclosed, so the exact contracted margin, and thus how much of the 8-10%+5-7% FCF accretion is locked in, is unknown.

Final cost and timing of the 433 MW Meta-funded nuclear uprates (<20% of capex by end-2028) and whether additional large-load deals at nuclear/gas sites are signed — Vistra's own forward-looking statements list 'potential transactions with large load facilities at our nuclear and natural gas plants' as pending, not done.
Extent of data-center onsite/self-generation adoption by 2030 (Bloom Energy/analysts estimate up to one-third), which would bypass Vistra's grid-supplied model.
Whether 2028 guidance (not yet initiated as of the Nov 6, 2026 release) embeds the Meta PPA ramp and Cogentrix contribution — the 3-year horizon ends with the least-visibility year.
what_would_change_the_view: Announcement (or conspicuous absence) of additional long-term PPAs with hyperscalers/large-load customers at Vistra's nuclear or gas sites — the company itself flags these as 'potential transactions'; a new multi-GW deal would strengthen the thesis, while none through 2027 would weaken it.

FERC/PJM decisions on extending or replacing the capacity price cap-and-collar beyond the 2027/2028 auction, or comparable Texas/ERCOT market redesign (e.g., a firm-shedding tariff or reliability product changes) that alters scarcity pricing.

ERCOT and PJM realized summer 2027 prices versus EIA's baseline vs high-demand scenarios (ERCOT 2027 baseline ~$47/MWh vs +$37/MWh in the high case) — observed prices near the high case would confirm the thesis; near baseline would undercut it.
Downward revisions to ERCOT/PJM official load forecasts or large cancellations of announced data-center projects (queue attrition), or a spike in data-center onsite generation announcements in Texas.

2028 guidance initiation: inclusion/exclusion of Meta PPA and uprate contributions, Cogentrix integration performance, and Moody's/S&P/Fitch rating actions on leverage (Moody's already moved its outlook to stable on the acquisitive strategy).
Execution of the Meta-funded nuclear uprates on schedule and budget (capex begins 2026, <20% spent by end-2028) — delays or cost overruns would push the contracted upside beyond the 3-year window.
